The Youth Climate Change Conference 2025 was successfully held from 4–5 November 2025 at the Emirates Hotel in Ondangwa, Oshana Region. The conference was convened under the theme: “Our Climate, Our Responsibility: Namibian Youth on Climate Action.” It brought together a wide and diverse representation, including government ministries, local authorities, academia, development partners, traditional leaders, media, youth leaders, learners, and children, totalling an estimated 157 participants. The event was spearheaded by SOS Children’s Villages Namibia through the Eco-Champions Project, with collaboration from partners and youth-led environmental organisations such as Youth4CAN, NAYORE, Tulonga Foundation, and Wakapinya Environmental Education.  The main objectives of the convening were to: Increase awareness among young people on climate change, its impacts, and their role in mitigation and adaptation, Build capacity through knowledge transfer on climate-smart practices, green entrepreneurship, climate finance, and resilience-building, Strengthen collaboration between youth and key stakeholders, including the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism, development agencies, academia, and local authorities, Provide a platform for youth-led dialogue, innovation, skills development, and policy advocacy and, Develop actionable commitments from youth and stakeholders towards climate resilience and sustainable development in Namibia. All these were achieved through presentations on various issues affecting youth and the environment, panel discussions, exhibitions to inspire youth to become innovators of ideas and break-out sessions tailored to create dialogues amongst youth on climate change mitigation.   Read more: https://youthforcan.org.na/2025/11/21/youth-climate-change-conference-namibia-2025/

World Hippo Day 🦛   Namibia’s rivers and wetlands are home to one of Africa’s most powerful and fascinating giants: the hippopotamus. Found in river systems like the Kunene, Kavango, Kwando and Zambezi, hippos play a vital role in maintaining healthy aquatic ecosystems.   As Namibia continues to champion community-based conservation, protecting hippos also means protecting livelihoods, biodiversity, and the delicate balance of our shared landscapes.   Let’s celebrate these incredible water giants and commit to safeguarding the wetlands and rivers they depend on.    #WorldHippoDay #NamibiaWildlife #CBNRM #ProtectOurWetlands #CommunityConservation

World Pangolin Day | 21 February   Today, Namibia joins the world in celebrating one of nature’s most unique and most threatened species: the pangolin. These shy, scale-covered mammals play a vital role in controlling insect populations and maintaining healthy ecosystems.  In Namibia, pangolins face growing threats from illegal wildlife trade and habitat loss.   Protecting them means protecting our biodiversity and supporting the community-led conservation efforts that make our country a global leader in conservation.  Let’s stand together to protect Namibia’s pangolins because when we protect wildlife, we protect our future.🌎  #WorldPangolinDay #ProtectPangolins #NamibiaWildlife #CBNRM #ConservationNamibia

LEGAL HUB: Minister Indileni Daniel on Friday launched the Sustainable Wildlife Management Programme Legal Hub in Windhoek, describing it as a strategic step forward in strengthening Namibia’s policy and legal framework for sustainable management of natural resources.   The hub is a website containing a collection of policy and legal documents relating to the governance and regulation of natural resources in Namibia. Namibia joins other countries with similar hubs, such as Botswana, Zambia and Zimbabwe, to mention a few.   The online hub is a central repository of information pertaining wildlife management laws that can be a dependable resource for scholars, practitioners, journalists and broader public. It was done in collaboration with FAO Namibia.

To reach rhinos in Kunene’s most remote areas, Save the Rhino Trust Namibia uses a Mule Patrol Unit. Combining the speed of horses with the sure-footed endurance of donkeys, these mules carry trackers, binoculars, GPS units, and cameras across rocky passes, gullies, and soft dunes far beyond vehicle access.  As staff say, they have adapted to the desert “like a mule to the desert,” helping rangers follow rhino trails across once-inaccessible wilderness. Real data. Real rangers. Real impact.  In 2023, Save the Rhino Trust (SRT), in partnership with Wadappt, introduced the Rhino Guardianship Certificate, a verified, performance-based approach to conservation funding.  Each certificate is backed by real field data collected by rangers, from rhino sightings to kilometres walked, and linked directly to the individual behind the effort.  For over 40 years, SRT has shown that boots on the ground make the difference. Now, that impact can be measured, verified, and supported. MEETING: Hon. Minister Indileni Daniel convened a meeting with the Namibia National Farmers Union and other stakeholders on Wednesday at the MEFT Headquarters in Windhoek to address issues surrounding Human-Wildlife Conflict.  Discussions centred on growing concerns over increasing elephant populations in the northern regions, with farmers reporting widespread crop destruction, damaged fencing, and loss to general infrastructure. Minister Daniel acknowledged these challenges and assured attendees that further engagements will be held to develop sustainable and collaborative solutions moving forward.

Weekly Teacher Spotlight!  My name is Helena Frans. I was born and raised in Iishanaputa Uukolonkadhi, a small village in the Omusati region. I started my schooling at Iishanaputa Combined School from Grade 1 to 10, and completed my secondary education (Grade 11–12) at Mwaala High School.  Due to financial challenges, my parents could no longer afford for me to continue my studies. I stayed at home and began searching for work. In 2021, my uncle called me from the north to come stay with his daughter at Naankuse Lodge.   In 2023, a daycare was opened on the farm for all the babies, and I continued working as a house helper for my uncle. I didn’t give up.   A few months later, a vacancy for a school cleaner opened at Naankuse Primary School. I submitted my CV, and within a week, I was told I could start the following Monday. That’s where my journey truly began in 2023.   I didn’t stop at cleaning, I also helped in the daycare, assisted teachers with marking learners’ test papers, and supported learners with their homework. In October 2024, during a meeting with our boss, Mrs. Marlice van Vuuren, we were asked where we see ourselves in five years.  I shared my dream of becoming a teacher. My colleagues supported me because they had seen my passion and dedication, especially how I worked with learners and assisted in the Grade 1 class. As of June 2025, I was appointed as a Grade 0 & 1 Class Assistant.   In January 2026, I began my role as a pre-primary teacher. In February 2026, I joined Alison online learning and earned two certificates in Early Childhood Development.   I still dream of studying further and becoming a graduate. I believe my skills, dedication, and willingness to learn make me a strong future leader. I am proud of my journey and excited to keep growing with the Naankuse family.  Stories like Helena’s are made possible through support and opportunity. If you would like to help us continue investing in education and changing lives, you can support the Naankuse Foundation Schools here: https://naankusefoundation.salsalabs.org/naankuseprimaryschool0/index.html

Protected Habitat Funded entirely by Tourism  The Okonjima Nature Reserve was created to secure protected habitat for wildlife, funded entirely through tourism.  It provides a rare opportunity to study wildlife in a well-protected, enclosed ecosystem over long timeframes.  AfriCat’s research within the Reserve helps assess how enclosed protected areas contribute to conservation, how species coexist, and how management decisions affect long-term ecological health.  What we learn here contributes to conservation thinking far beyond Okonjima.  #africat #okonjima #leopard #ConservationScience #WildlifeResearch  ____  © @pascal__ok

30 seconds of Tupuka in the wild, without trending audio. 🐆  Estimated to be approximately five-years-old, Tupuka was captured on a farm in Namibia in August and returned to the wild in September. Before being released, Tupuka was fitted with a tracking collar as part of our Early Warning System (EWS) program. Relying on GPS satellite collars equipped with geofencing functions, the program uses virtual fences to alert farmers when cheetahs are on their land. These real-time warnings allow farmers to protect their livestock using non-lethal methods - helping to keep cheetahs like Tupuka in the wild.   #cheetah #cheetahconservation #fahlo

Meet our Cheetah of the Month, Aidan! Aidan was rescued in Somaliland in August. He was one of ten cubs confiscated from wildlife traffickers, thanks to collaborative efforts of Somaliland’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change (MoECC) and Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF). At the time of his rescue, Aidan was estimated to be approximately seven months old. As one of the older cubs in the group, the young cubs looked to Aidan for comfort and reassurance.   After being rescued, Aidan and the other cubs were transferred to the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC) in Geed-Deeble. He was very dehydrated and malnourished when he arrived, and staff provided intensive care to prevent re-feeding syndrome and help Aidan build up his strength. After being tied up in captivity for months, Aidan also had difficulty walking. However, with specialized, round-the-clock care, Aidan was stabilized, gradually built up strength and began to thrive. In 2025, he was named by entrepreneur and philanthropist Simon Squibb (@simonsquibb), in honor of his son.   Today, Aidan lives in a large and naturalistic enclosure at the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC), where he is continuing his rehabilitation. 400km in 14 days… This bull taught us a lot!  Bull 6, now nicknamed “Etosha Boy”, was collared during our January operation. As a young adult male, he’s part of a group that often travels widely, exploring new areas and shaping movement pathways across the landscape.  Within just 14 days, he covered over 400 km, moving from our area of operation into Etosha, and has since wandered back out again, now recorded east of Outjo.  We still haven’t managed to get ID photos of him ourselves. Instead, we’re tracking his journey through collar data and the photos shared by farmers whose land he passes through.  Movements like his teach us a lot about how elephants use the landscape, how they respond to changing conditions, and how connectivity between areas matters more than ever, especially as climate and habitats shift. Understanding these patterns is key to adapting coexistence strategies for the future 🐘

Lately, most conversations around elephants in Namibia have been shaped by conflict. Crops destroyed, water points damaged, and in some cases, lives lost.  These are real and serious situations, and they deserve attention.  But at the same time, there is another side to this story that is often missed.  Across the country, people are learning how to live alongside elephants in a more informed and practical way. Not because it’s easy, but because it’s necessary.  One of the biggest shifts we see through EHRA’s PEACE Project is how quickly fear changes when understanding grows. Many participants arrive thinking elephants are unpredictable and dangerous. After the training, that perception often shifts.  As one participant shared: “I always thought elephants wanted to hurt you. But now I understand they don’t, if we don’t threaten them.”  Understanding behaviour, what attracts elephants, and what triggers them, can make a real difference in how situations are handled, especially in places where people are moving through elephant habitat every day.

A long period of energy anxiety and power interruptions, with downstream damage to equipment, is eventually coming to an end. When drought dries up water sources, pressure rises for both people and elephants. They end up relying on the same scarce resources, and conflict becomes more likely.  For elders living remotely, like Ouma Elsie, this becomes a reality. Failed rains, damaged gardens, and elephants searching for food and water can quickly threaten a household’s stability.  Ouma Elsie has always adapted and persevered, like many rural residents do. But some challenges need extra support. EHRA assisted with a water tank, a solar pump, and garden protection to reduce risk and ease daily pressure.  Her garden was one of the first we ever attempted to protect. The wall helped, but it also taught us that some methods work better than others. Conservation often means testing, learning and improving as we go. Today, electric fencing has proven far more effective for garden protection.  Coexistence is not a fixed formula. It’s a process of listening, adjusting and working alongside communities who live with elephants every day 🐘  📽️: @conservation.diaries

Statement by Elephant-Human Relations Aid (EHRA):  Elephant-Human Relations Aid (EHRA) would like to address the recently published announcement regarding an elephant bull that damaged the roof of a house in Okongwe.  During the night, EHRA’s Elephant Guards responded immediately and successfully chased the bull away before the situation escalated further. Fortunately, no one was sleeping in the house at the time, and no injuries occurred.  The bull was attracted by Ana tree seed pods stored inside the house. Ana seed pods are a natural and highly preferred food source for elephants. They attract elephants much like sweets attract children. When seed pods or livestock feed are stored inside homes, this creates a known and significant risk of attracting elephants, especially during dry periods when their preferred food is scarce in riverbeds.  In situations like this, if there is no rapid response and preventative action, frustration and fear can quickly escalate, placing both people and elephants at risk.   The following day, EHRA arranged and funded the repair work, ensuring that members of the local community were employed to rebuild the damaged roof. We also convened an emergency meeting with residents to discuss the risks associated with storing seed pods inside living spaces and to explore safer storage solutions.  We strongly encourage residents not to store seed pods or livestock feed in structures where people sleep. If storage is necessary, it should be located away from sleeping areas and secured as safely as possible.  Desert-dwelling elephants are a protected and globally significant population, and their long-term survival depends on effective conflict mitigation rather than reactive measures.  EHRA will continue to share Early Warning Alerts with all residents. Our Elephant Guards remain on call to respond to conflict situations and to assist community members who feel unsafe or need help protecting their property.  For coexistence advice or emergency assistance, please contact a local EHRA Elephant Guard by the numbers given above.

This inspiring group of women started a community garden to help feed their community, with a special focus on supporting local pensioners.  Living and farming in an elephant area comes with real challenges, so the group asked for protection and practical training. Over the course of this year, EHRA has supported the project with solar lights, a protection wall around their water tank (funded by AGA), and most recently, a three-day human–elephant coexistence training at our Education Centre, made possible with support from @zooberlin.  While the elephants had moved out of the area during the training, learning continued in another powerful way. A visit to the protected vegetable garden at Irene Pos allowed for valuable peer-to-peer exchange. Geraldine, a Damara resident, shared her experience of living alongside elephants, explaining how her electric fence works, how bee sounds are used as a deterrent, and how sharing water has helped reduce conflict in her village.  A meaningful few days of learning, sharing, and women supporting women.

SRT was founded in 1982 to protect the last black rhinos of Kunene and Erongo. What began with Blythe Loutit, a single Land Rover and the sale of her artwork soon grew into community-led patrols that helped curb poaching. By 1986, SRT supported three tracking teams and ten community game guards, backed by a structured monitoring system.  SRT later built the world’s longest-running photographic and life-history database of black rhinos, a cornerstone of conservation in the region.  #SaveTheRhino #Humblebeginnings #RhinoConservation

Community development is at the heart of SRT’s work. CONRAD (NAD) BRAIN 1963 - 2025  Today, Gobabeb staff and associates, past and present, honour one of our own, a remarkable Namibian soul – a wildlife vet, scientist, and pilot whose life was inextricably woven into the land he loved. Having been introduced to the Namib at an early age, Nad dedicated his days to the wild places of Namibia, more recently rekindling his association with Gobabeb.  Whether planning new projects to investigate longevity and health of the keystone fig trees in the Kuiseb, advising young postgraduate students on baboon behaviour, imagining the adventures of a very famous 4x4 hero, brainstorming ideas to ensure sustainability of the research facility, or lifting into the sky to track gemsbok from above, he lived with purpose, courage, and quiet generosity. But beyond these professional roles, he was simply a good man – kind, and impossibly humble. He gave without hesitation, without needing thanks. A subtle hint, and he had our students up the air on their first flying experience. A small gesture, perhaps, but leaving a huge and lasting affection for that tall, bare-footed, friendly figure in dusty overalls striding across the gravel plains en route to the airfield.  Today we celebrate a life lived boldly and compassionately. Though he has taken his final flight, his presence circles above us still — in the Namib Desert he loved, the wilderness he protected, and the lives he touched.

Did you know that around 20% of the world’s arid and hyper-arid regions are covered by aeolian dunes? Despite their vast extent, the processes controlling how these dunes form and evolve are still not fully understood. At Gobabeb, we are helping to narrow this knowledge gap by collecting detailed field measurements through the TOAD HARE project. The project investigates how surface roughness elements, such as vegetation, influence wind-driven sand transport across desert landscapes. By improving how wind–sand interactions are represented in models, this work contributes to better monitoring of dune dynamics and a clearer understanding of their origins. #desertlandscapes #namibdesert #dunes #geomorphology

Jabulani & Naleli 😻  Previously, we followed Jabulani’s transition from a northern-born cub to a southern resident male. Over the past year, he has consolidated his territory and grown increasingly confident within it. Naleli’s story unfolded alongside his. A young female establishing herself in the same southern region, she has secured her own space as she approaches reproductive maturity.  As both leopards strengthened their presence, their movements began to align. If successful, this union would connect long-standing northern and southern maternal lines within the Reserve. Selene returns with a surprise 😍  Selene is a female pangolin first tagged in April 2021 as part of AfriCat’s early pangolin research. Over the following years, she was recorded giving birth and contributed rare insight into pangolin life history.  In late 2023, her GPS stopped working, and her VHF tag fell off. With no signal to follow, Selene was lost from the research. Equipment failure and the loss of monitored individuals are an unavoidable part of pangolin research and can create significant data gaps.  Nearly two years later, on 13 November 2025, Selene was re-identified after one of AfriCat’s pangolin trackers, Jacob, observed two pangolins emerging from a burrow, both without tags. One was a male whose tag had fallen off weeks earlier. The second was Selene, identified by her scale patterns. And she wasnt alone…she was accompanied by a pup on her back weighing 425g.  Her reappearance highlights the challenges of studying pangolins while reconnecting an interrupted research record and adding a new chapter to her story.  IMPORTANT NOTICE:  Pangolin welfare remains a high conservation priority. Recent data indicates escalating pangolin trafficking activity throughout Namibia, requiring enhanced surveillance protocols for our monitored population. We maintain regular visual confirmation of all tagged individuals to ensure their continued safety and wellbeing. This mother-offspring pair has been successfully observed during multiple subsequent field surveys, with both animals demonstrating positive health and behavioral indicators.  #africat #pangolin #research #wildlifeconservation #namibia

Happy International Hyena Day 🐺  Today, we celebrate one of Africa’s most misunderstood and often vilified carnivores, the brown hyena. Long entangled in folklore and misconception, it is far more than the stories suggest. This is a highly adapted scavenger-predator, quietly shaping nutrient flows, recycling biomass, and linking predator communities across Namibia’s landscapes in ways that often go unseen.  At Okonjima Nature Reserve, long-term research is steadily reshaping how this species is understood. What emerges is a picture of complexity: structured clans moving across shared landscapes, individuals ranging over vast distances at night, and close ecological interactions with other large carnivores, particularly leopard, where feeding opportunities briefly concentrate life across the system.  Through GPS tracking, camera trapping, and sustained field observation, Africat is revealing a species that is rarely encountered yet constantly active within the ecosystem.  Stay tuned for an update on our Brown Hyena Project later this week…  #africat #research #wildlifeconservation #hyena #okonjima  ___© @pascal__ok

This week, a project from visiting scientists led by Manuel Herzog from the University of Heidelberg took us deep into the dunes to study star dunes, also known as mega-dunes. These impressive formations develop under complex wind regimes, where strong winds from multiple directions shape and reshape the dunes over time. The team collected sand samples from the top and carried out detailed laser measurements to monitor crest movement and surface changes. An additional sampling site includes Sossusvlei, with plans for repeated visits over the coming years to build a long-term dataset. We look forward to continuing collaboration and to the new insights this research will bring into dune dynamics.

ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS: Environment, Forestry and Tourism Minister Indileni Daniel is leading the Namibian delegation at the seventh session of the UN Environment Assembly (UNEA-7), under way in Nairobi, Kenya.  On the sidelines of the UNEA-7, Minister Daniel met with officials from Oxytane International Limited, a firm offering countries a practical pathway to accelerate progress towards their climate commitments by supporting early compliance with future emissions standards, reducing fossil-fuel consumption and lowering greenhouse-gas emissions.  Namibia, despite its negligible contribution to global carbon emissions, continues to bear the brunt of climate-change impacts, including recurring droughts and floods. The Ministry, in collaboration with the South Africa National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) and BirdLife South Africa, is hosting a regional workshop focused on advancing Key Biodiversity Area (KBA) identification and application in Southern Africa. The workshop brings together biodiversity scientists, conservation practitioners, policy experts, and data specialists from Namibia, South Africa, Malawi, and Mozambique under the Spatial Biodiversity Assessment, Prioritization and Planning (SBAPP) Regional Project to strengthen technical expertise in identifying, mapping, and managing the most important sites for biodiversity. Supported by AFD and FFEM, this initiative enhances regional collaboration, supports national conservation planning, and contributes to global biodiversity goals under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

South Africa topped as Namibia’s leading African tourist source market in 2024, while Germany remained the biggest overseas source markets. Out of Her Mother’s Shadow | Naleli   Meet Naleli, a young leopard in the emerging cohort of female leopards, navigating the pivotal transition from maternal dependence to establishing her own territory.  Born in late 2022 to Lila, the dominant female of the Reserve’s south, Naleli first appeared in our records in April 2023 alongside a sibling that was sadly lost later that year. Initially cautious and seldom seen, she gradually became more tolerant of human observation, likely influenced by her mother’s regular presence. As her dispersal began, she revealed an unexpected aptitude for exploiting small structural gaps, repeatedly entering and exiting fenced sections of the Reserve. even pulling her first small prey items through the same spaces.  Today, Naleli occupies the southern portion of Lila’s home range, while her sister Vamos has settled to the north. This spatial arrangement allows their mother to maintain proximity to both daughters.   As Naleli consolidates her territory and gains independence, she stands at the threshold of reproductive maturity, representing the next generation of leopards that will continue the legacy of Okonjima’s iconic big cats.
